stories.headline: AI BUBBLE FEARS TRIGGER NASDAQ-100'S WORST SESSION SINCE JUNE
stories.body: The Nasdaq 100 sank 2.50% to 29,187.55 and the S&P 500 fell 1.09% to 7,659.44 as a global tech selloff, sparked by weakness in Korea's chip-heavy KOSPI, spread to Wall Street on renewed doubts about AI capital spending. The Nasdaq is now down more than 4% on the week, its worst since June.
stories.explain: Mega-cap tech names carry outsized weight in both indices, so any repricing of AI-related capex (debt-funded data center buildouts, chip orders) moves the whole market even when the news is sector-specific. Investors are increasingly questioning whether the hundreds of billions being spent on AI infrastructure will generate matching returns, and that doubt compresses the high multiples those stocks trade at. Because the Nasdaq 100 is cap-weighted, a handful of AI-exposed giants falling 4-5% can drag the whole index down 2%+ even when market breadth is only modestly negative.

stories.headline: 10-YEAR YIELD HOLDS NEAR 5.07% AS FLIGHT TO SAFETY OFFSETS HOT CPI
stories.body: The 10-year Treasury yield slipped 1 basis point to 5.07%, well off the 5.3%+ spike hit just two days earlier after September's hotter-than-expected CPI print. The pullback came as investors rotated out of equities and into bonds during today's tech-led risk-off move.
stories.explain: Normally a hot CPI report pushes yields higher because it raises the odds the Fed holds rates higher for longer. But when a sharp equity selloff hits at the same time, a 'flight to quality' bid for Treasuries can dominate, pushing bond prices up and yields down even as the inflation backdrop argues for the opposite. That tug-of-war, inflation data pulling yields up while risk-off flows pull them down, is exactly what produced this week's round trip from above 5.3% to 5.07%.

stories.headline: WTI SURGES 3.4% TO $101 ON HORMUZ TENSIONS, STEEP INVENTORY DRAW
stories.body: WTI crude jumped $3.40, or 3.4%, to $101.34 a barrel (Brent near $109.44) after fresh tension around the Strait of Hormuz and an EIA report showing U.S. crude inventories fell 8.6 million barrels in the week ended October 9, well above consensus.
stories.explain: The Strait of Hormuz carries roughly a fifth of global oil flows, so any perceived threat to shipping there adds a geopolitical risk premium independent of actual supply disruption. Layer on an inventory draw nearly double what traders expected, a signal of stronger demand or tighter domestic supply, and crude gets a two-sided catalyst: a risk premium plus a fundamentals surprise, which is why the move was so outsized relative to a typical session.

stories.headline: GOLD SLIPS AS TECH SELLOFF TRIGGERS CASH-RAISING, NOT A SAFE-HAVEN BID
stories.body: Spot gold eased about 0.4% to roughly $4,168 an ounce even as stocks sold off, a sign the metal is being used as a funding source rather than a hedge. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's refusal to rule out a rate hike also weighed on bullion.
stories.explain: Gold is supposed to rally when stocks fall, but that only holds when investors are rotating into havens rather than scrambling for cash. When a selloff is sharp enough to trigger margin calls, funds instead sell whatever is liquid, including gold, to raise cash and meet those calls, which can push gold down in the same session stocks are falling. A hawkish Fed signal compounds that by raising the opportunity cost of holding a non-yielding asset like gold relative to cash or Treasuries.

stories.headline: $2 TRILLION DEFICIT, 5% YIELDS SEEN AS NEXT BIG FISCAL CHALLENGE
stories.body: Strategists are flagging the combination of a roughly $2 trillion annual federal deficit and Treasury yields sitting near 5% as a structural headwind, warning that debt-service costs are climbing even as the government must keep issuing more supply to cover the gap.
stories.explain: When yields rise, every dollar of maturing debt has to be refinanced at a higher rate, which mechanically increases the interest bill on outstanding debt with a lag. At a $2 trillion deficit, higher-for-longer yields don't just cost more directly, they also mean more new issuance is needed to fund that deficit, which itself puts upward pressure on yields by increasing bond supply, a dynamic some strategists worry can become self-reinforcing.

stories.headline: FLORIDA TABBED NO. 1 IN SEC PRESEASON MEDIA POLL AS AP TOP 25 NEARS RELEASE
stories.body: The SEC preseason media poll picked Florida to finish atop the conference, with Duke widely projected as the Gators' closest rival for the national No. 1 spot once the AP's preseason Top 25 drops later this month. The two meet Dec. 1 in Gainesville as part of the ACC/SEC Challenge, with the regular season set to tip off Nov. 2.

stories.headline: NBA CLUBS TRIM ROSTERS TO 15 AS SEASON-OPENING TRIPLEHEADER NEARS
stories.body: Teams finalized rosters Saturday ahead of Tuesday's three-game opening night, waiving the bulk of Exhibit 9 and 10 camp invitees; the Knicks cut guard Bruce Brown. Injuries already thinned a few rotations, Orlando's Noah Penda (partially torn hamstring) and Denver's Julian Strawther (six weeks, sprained knee) will open the season out, while Giannis Antetokounmpo gets set to debut with Miami Tuesday against Orlando.

stories.headline: TRADE FRENZY CONTINUES: GIANTS, STEELERS, EAGLES ALL MAKE MOVES BEFORE NOV. 10 DEADLINE
stories.body: Days after Arizona sent receiver Marvin Harrison Jr. to Houston, more dominoes fell: the Giants added quarterback J.J. McCarthy from Minnesota while Jaxson Dart recovers from knee surgery, Pittsburgh dealt cornerback Joey Porter Jr. to Dallas, and Philadelphia sent center Cam Jurgens to Baltimore. With three weeks left before the deadline, the Chargers' Khalil Mack and Jacksonville's Brian Thomas Jr. are the next names drawing interest.

stories.headline: NO. 8 BYU STUNS NO. 2 NOTRE DAME 28-24 IN WEEK 7'S WILDEST SATURDAY
stories.body: Bear Bachmeier's touchdown pass to Walker Lyons with 1:47 left lifted BYU to a 28-24 win over Notre Dame in Provo, the biggest win in program history and a result that reshapes the playoff picture. It capped a chaotic day of ranked matchups: Ohio State survived Indiana 19-15 (but lost QB Julian Sayin to a multi-week arm injury), Florida rallied from a 17-0 deficit to stun Texas 27-24, and Tennessee throttled Alabama 26-10, Bama's second straight loss for the first time since 2007.

deepDive.title: The Strait of Hormuz Risk Premium: Pricing Oil When Nothing Has Actually Happened Yet
content: Friday's WTI print, still on the board heading into this weekend, closed at $101 a barrel, up 6% on the week on two separate drivers layered together: an 8.6-million-barrel inventory draw and fresh tension around the Strait of Hormuz. Only one of those is a fundamentals story. The other is a bet on something that hasn't happened, no tanker has been seized, no barrel has actually failed to ship. For an econ student, that split matters, because it's one of the few places in markets where you can watch a pure geopolitical risk premium get priced in real time, separate from the physical supply-demand picture.

The premium gets built from three channels that move before any physical disruption occurs. War-risk insurance on tankers transiting the Strait spikes immediately, since underwriters reprice exposure the moment threat chatter rises, adding real cost per barrel shipped. Options markets show it as skew, traders bidding up out-of-the-money calls as cheap insurance against a supply shock, which pulls the forward curve's implied volatility higher even when spot barely moves. And OPEC+ spare capacity, roughly 4-5 million barrels a day sitting idle, acts as the cushion traders are implicitly pricing against, so the premium shrinks whenever that cushion looks adequate and swells when it looks thin.

What gets missed is that a geopolitical oil spike usually behaves like a short-term rental the market can't actually afford to keep paying, not a durable repricing. When drones hit Saudi Arabia's Abqaiq facility in September 2019, knocking out roughly 5% of global oil supply overnight, Brent jumped nearly 15% in a single session, the biggest intraday spike since the Gulf War. Within six weeks it had fully round-tripped back to pre-attack levels once Saudi Arabia restored production faster than feared and spare capacity proved sufficient. The lesson: a risk premium decays almost as fast as it's built unless the underlying threat actually escalates into a realized supply loss.

The current $101 print is harder to read than Abqaiq because it bundles a real, measurable leg (that inventory draw) with a speculative one (Hormuz), and only the first is durable if tensions cool. Chris's useful exercise heading into next week is watching whether WTI gives back ground on any de-escalation headline, which would reveal how much of this move is premium versus how much reflects genuinely tight physical balances. A premium that unwinds quickly has limited inflation implications for the Fed's next CPI read; a supply-driven leg that holds does not, and that distinction is exactly what the bond market was already fighting over on Friday.
